title: Tumours and Tumour-Like Conditions of Oral Cavity and Facial Region

blocks.text: Tumours and Tumour-Like Conditions of Oral Cavity and Facial Region
Benign Odontogenic Tumors
Each tumour presents with different cardinal features clinically, radiologically and on histopathological diagnosis.
Ameloblastoma
Clinical Presentation
Recognized between ages of 10 to 80 years80% form in the mandible and 70% develop in the posterior molar region and often involve the ramus

runs.text: Recognized between ages of 10 to 80 years80%

blocks.text: Painless, slow growing tumor that may be solid or cystic
Loosening of teeth, with roots resorption
Gradual facial asymmetry due to enlargement and destruction of bone

runs.text: Gradual facial asymmetry due to enlargement

blocks.text: Ping pong and/or bone cracking effects
Investigations
Radiographically, the tumour presents with multilocular radiolucency, honeycomb, or soap bubble appearance.

Note: Diagnostic confirmation of this tumour is through histopathology. Complete excision e.g. e.g. marginal resection, segmental resection plus bone grafting and partial or total resection of the jaw is the treatment of choice. Hence refer the patient to the center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon

blocks.text: Calcifying odontogenic tumor Clinical Presentation
Most often found in the mandibular molar/premolar region, but 33% of cases are found in the maxilla
It is associated with an unerupted or impacted tooth in 50% of cases
Investigations
Radiographically these lesions can be radiolucent, but more characteristically are mixed lucent and opaque masses, exhibiting a snow-driven appearance

runs.text: opaque masses, exhibiting a snow-driven appearance

blocks.text: Non-Pharmacological Management
Complete excision of the tumour with border of normal bone should be curative, but curettage or incomplete excision has high recurrence rates.

runs.text: Complete excision of the tumour with border of normal bone should be curative, but curettage or incomplete

blocks.text: Amelobastic Fibroma Clinical Presentation
Slower growing tumor than the simple ameloblastoma and does not infiltrate between bone trabeculae.
Occurs during the first two decades of life
75% of ameloblastic fibromas are found in the posterior mandible in the area of a developing tooth. It is benign and expansile, growing as a pushing front rather than invading surrounding tissues

runs.text: benign and expansile, growing as a pushing front rather than invading surrounding tissues

blocks.text: Investigations
Radiographically this lesion appears as a uniocular or bilocular radiolucency, most often in the posterior mandible.

The radiographic appearance is identical to that of unicystic ameloblastoma, and both lesions should be differential diagnoses because they affect similar age groups and have similar clinical and radiographic appearances. Histologic examination differentiates the two.

runs.text: be differential diagnoses because they affect similar age groups and have similar clinical and radiographic appearances. Histologic examination differentiates the two.

blocks.text: Non-Pharmacological Management

Enucleation and curettage and extraction of associated teeth is usually adequate for small tumours. For big tumours conservative resection may be required, where necessary to be followed with reconstruction.

runs.text: big tumours conservative resection may be required, where necessary to be followed with reconstruction.

blocks.text: Adenomatoid odontogenic Tumors (AOT) Clinical Presentation.
Usually occur in the second and third decades
Usually encountered incidentally
It has a female predilection
Two thirds of the cases occur in the anterior maxilla, one third occur in the anterior mandible, and it is never found posterior to the premolars

runs.text: never found posterior to the premolars

blocks.text: Two thirds of the cases are associated with an impacted tooth (usually the cuspid) Present with mild swelling or in association with a clinically missing tooth

runs.text: or in association with a clinically missing tooth

blocks.text: Investigations

Radiographically this lesion generally appears as a well-demarcated radiolucency. In 75% of cases, it is associated with an unerupted tooth, usually the canine. It may contain radiopaque flecks, which represent calcified material.

runs.text: an unerupted tooth, usually the canine. It may contain radiopaque flecks, which represent calcified material.

blocks.text: Non-Pharmacological Management
Enucleation is curative and recurrence is almost unknown.
Odontogenic Myxoma Clinical Presentation
Occurs mostly in the second to fourth decades of life
Clinically indistinguishable from ameloblastoma, but on aspiration while ameloblastoma yields
straw-colored or yellow fluid Odontogenic myxoma may not yield anything due to the thick mucoid clear contents of the tumour.
The radiographic appearance; typically, it has honeycomb appearance, although
It often appears quite like ameloblastoma e.g multilocular radiolucency
Investigations
OPG, CBCT, Tissue biopsy (Confirmation is through histopathology)
Non-Pharmacological Management
Wide surgical excision Similar approach to the treatment of ameloblastoma. It has a high recurrence rate if not completely removed.
Cemento-ossious lesions

These are groups of benign fibro-osseous lesions that affect the jawbones, particularly the tooth-bearing areas. These lesions involve replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue that contains varying amounts of mineralized material (bone, cementum, or both).
Clinical Presentation
Commonly occurring in the posterior region of the mandible,
Occurs mainly in females of African origin aged between 40 and 50 years.
Three main types:
Periapical
Focal and
Florid.
Periapical type is usually seen in the anterior mandible,
Focal type is usually involving single teeth in the posterior mandible
Florid type is seen all quadrants but mainly in the posterior part of the mandible.
Generally symptomless and are incidentally diagnosed during routine radiographic examinations.
Investigations
Radiographically ranging from radioluscencies, mixed radioluscent-radioopaque, and completely radiopaque lesions.
Non-Pharmacological Management
They are only treated when they produce symptoms, interfere with other dental treatments or when infected.
When surgery is indicated, complete enucleation is necessary.
Pharmacological Management
Management is similar to chronic osteomyelitis above
Odontoma (Compound and Complex)
This is a developmental malformation made up of enamel, dentin, cementum, and pulp (odontogenic tissues) and is considered a hamartoma. It is the most common odontogenic tumours.

runs.text: It is the most common odontogenic tumours.

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation
Normally discovered incidentally during routine dental examinations or radiographs
Missing eruption of the permanent tooth
They can occur anywhere in the jaws but mainly in the anterior maxilla (compound) and posterior mandible (complex).
Vary in size but can grow to huge lesions
Investigation
Periapical X-ray, OPG, CBCT
Generally, the lesions appear radiopaque with compound type appears as a collection of tooth-like structures, whereas the complex type appears as a disorganized mass of dental tissues.

runs.text: complex type appears as a disorganized mass of dental tissues.

blocks.text: Management
Surgical (Enucleation)
Non-Odontogenic Benign Tumours
Pregnancy Tumours (also called pyogenic granuloma)
Clinical Presentation
Not a true tumour, but rather a rapid over growth of tissue in response to local irritation.
They most commonly appear after first trimester, grow rapidly, and typically regress after delivery.
Found on the gingiva mainly in between the teeth. Occasionally can occur on the tongue, lips and palate.
They are exophytic, lobulated, or smooth surfaced lesion with a red to purplish color and a soft, spongy texture and easily bleed
Non-Pharmacological Management

Surgical intervention is often not required. However, pregnancy tumors can be removed during the second trimester if they interfere with occlusion, are painful, bleed excessively, or are excessively large. Lesions excised during pregnancy often recur.
After delivery, pregnancy tumors typically recede spontaneously but excision may be necessary for those cases which persist.

blocks.text: Note: Other non- odontogenic tumors are Osteomas, Myxomas, Chondromas, Central giant cell and Fibro-osteoma.
Benign Soft Tissues Non-Odontogenic Tumours
Head and Neck Vascular lesions (Vascular anomalies)

These are a group of disorders involving abnormal development or growth of blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) or lymphatic vessels. Classified into two main groups hemangiomas and vascular malformations

runs.text: or lymphatic vessels. Classified into two main groups hemangiomas and vascular malformations

S/N
Feature
Hemangioma
Vascular Malformation
Time of Presentation
Present at birth; most diagnosed by 1 year of age
Present at birth but often not diagnosed until second decade
Growth Pattern
Rapid growth up to 6–8 months, then slows and involutes by 5–9 years

Pathophysiology
Neoplastic growth with increased endothelial cell turnover
Growth due to abnormal flow dynamics and recruitment of collateral vessels
Osseous Involvement
Rare
Common (~35%)
Sex Distribution
Female-to-male ratio ≈ 5:1
Female-to-male ratio ≈ 2:1
Flow Characteristics
Usually low-flow lesion
May be low-flow (capillary, venous, lymphatic) or high-flow (arterial or arteriovenous)

US ultrasound,

Management

Currently, various medical and surgical options are available for the treatment of hemangiomas. In Tanzania we recommend Intralesional bleomycin injections (IL-Bleo) under Ultrasound guidance as the management of choice of head and neck hemangiomas.

Malignant Soft and Bone Tumours
Oral squamous cell carcinoma
Clinical Presentation
A sore in the mouth that does not heal (most common symptom).
Pain in the mouth.
Persistent lump or thickening of mucosa in the cheek.
Persistent white or red patch on the tongue, gums, tonsils, or lining of the mouth.

runs.text: tongue, gums, tonsils, or lining of the mouth.

blocks.text: Difficult moving jaw or tongue.
Difficult chewing or swallowing.
Enlarged cervical lymph nodes may be present

Note: Take a tissue biopsy of the lesion and send for histopathology investigation or refer the patient as early as possible to a center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon and Histopathology unit.

runs.text: possible to a center where there is oral and maxillofacial surgeon and Histopathology unit.

blocks.text: Management
Depending on the stage of tumor, management include; wide tumour excision (stage I, II, and III) and neck dissection followed by radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

runs.text: dissection followed by radiotherapy or chemotherapy.

blocks.text: For stage IV tumor; depending with general condition of the patient, management may range from palliative chemotherapy or radiotherapy or radio-chemotherapy.

runs.text: palliative chemotherapy or radiotherapy or radio-chemotherapy.

blocks.text: Oral Kaposi’s Sarcoma
Oral Kaposi’s Sarcoma (OKS) is a malignant angioproliferative tumour of endothelial origin involving the oral cavity. It is caused by infection with Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).

runs.text: is caused by infection with Human Herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).

blocks.text: It commonly occurs in the context of advanced HIV-related immunodepression and may represent the first manifestation of HIV infection.
Clinical Presentation
slow- to fast-growing masses
May appear as ecchymotic patches, nodular, and exophytic lesions presenting a color that can vary from dark reddish to purplish blue

runs.text: vary from dark reddish to purplish blue

blocks.text: Most frequently affected intra-oral sites are the hard-palatal mucosa and the gingiva
Size of the lesions varies from few millimeters to some centimeters and the growing of multiple lesions could lead to large, confluent masses involving an entire area of the oral cavity

runs.text: multiple lesions could lead to large, confluent masses involving an entire area of the oral cavity

blocks.text: Management.
Local surgery and highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) are considered keystones in the management of epidemic KS
Note: For detailed management of KS please refer to the malignancy on chapter twenty-two
Lymphomas
These are group of neoplasms of varying degrees of malignancy which are derived from B-cells of lymphoid tissues, the lymphocytes and histiocytes in any of their developmental stages.

runs.text: the lymphocytes and histiocytes in any of their developmental stages.

blocks.text: While lymphoma primarily affects lymph nodes, it can also occur in non-lymph node tissue (tonsils, parotid gland, thyroid gland, tongue, paranasal sinuses, and nasal cavity), this is known as extra nodal lymphoma

runs.text: gland, tongue, paranasal sinuses, and nasal cavity), this is known as extra nodal lymphoma

blocks.text: Lymphoma is classified as Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Both types of Lymphoma have similar symptoms which may include but not limited to painless swelling of lymph nodes, fever, Night sweats, Unexplained weight loss, and fatigue

runs.text: fever, Night sweats, Unexplained weight loss, and fatigue

blocks.text: Burkitt’s lymphoma (African Jaw Lymphoma)

Burkitt lymphoma is an aggressive non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma characterized by rapid tumor growth, frequently affecting the jaw, abdomen, or central nervous system associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

runs.text: the jaw, abdomen, or central nervous system associated with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

blocks.text: Three clinical subtypes: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-related. The endemic form, common in Africa, is linked to malaria and EBV,

runs.text: Three clinical subtypes: endemic, sporadic, and immunodeficiency-related. The endemic form, common in Africa, is linked to malaria and EBV,

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation
Confined almost exclusively to children between 2–14years of age.
Rapidly growing tumor mass of the jaws, destroying the bone and causing teeth loosening with extension the maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses as well as the orbit.

runs.text: with extension the maxillary, ethmoid and sphenoid sinuses as well as the orbit.

blocks.text: Visceral organ involvement may occur.
Malignant Salivary glands tumours
These are malignancies arising from major salivary glands (parotid gland, submandibular gland, sublingual gland) and minor salivary glands of the upper aerodigestive tract.

runs.text: These are malignancies arising from major salivary glands (parotid gland, submandibular gland, sublingual gland) and minor salivary glands of the upper aerodigestive tract.

blocks.text: The most common malignant salivary glands tumours include mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC), acinic cell carcinoma (ACC), adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC), carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma (CExPA), and adenocarcinoma.

runs.text: (ACC), adenoid cystic carcinoma (AdCC), carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma (CExPA), and adenocarcinoma.

blocks.text: Clinical Presentation.
Asymptomatic, firm mass with occasional pain and facial paralysis
Some presents with ulceration
Investigations
Ultrasound is the first non- invasive option for evaluating major salivary gland tumors

runs.text: Ultrasound is the first non- invasive

blocks.text: Computerized tomography (CT)
Management
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)
Open tissue biopsy
Mainstay treatment of salivary gland malignancies is surgery (wide tumour excision and neck dissection) followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy.

Note: Diagnostic confirmation is through histopathology; hence, it is emphasized to do early detection and referral to all patients suspected to have head and neck malignancies. (For detailed management of malignant tumors please refer to the malignancy on chapter twenty-two)
